What will Donald Trump do with the remaining two years of his presidency, and how will Democrats in Congress respond? On Washington Week With The Atlantic , panelists joined to discuss this and more
A Democrat-controlled Congress will soon have the chance to act on many of the issues that brought people out to vote, panelists explained last night

Issues such as the war in Iran, immigration, and the president’s use of the National Guard are among the “central touchpoints that we’ve seen over the last couple of years that have really driven people to anger, and to the polls,” Adam Harris, the host of Radio Atlantic , argued

And although some people will say that the results of the midterms are “retribution from Democrats,” he added, “a lot of voters will say it’s accountability.” Joining the editor in chief of The Atlantic , Jeffrey Goldberg, to discuss this and more: Peter Baker, a chief White House correspondent at The New York Times ; Leigh Ann Caldwell, a chief Washington correspondent at Puck ; Stephen Hayes, the editor and CEO of The Dispatch ; and Harris

title: Memories of the Train
excerpt: Illustrations by Katherine Lam The train’s seats : blue with a white strip down the middle
body: Illustrations by Katherine Lam The train’s seats : blue with a white strip down the middle
He was playing with the top his mother had bought from the cart lady
With each spin came flashes of rainbow light: zzz zzz zoom
The train’s seats: white with a blue strip down the middle, five per row
A hard orange sunlight cut through the glass
He was playing with the top his mother had bought
With each spin came flashes of rainbow light: zzz zzz zoom
The train’s seats: mostly blue and a little white, five per row
Earlier Dudu, giggling, had knocked over the top
Their mother, before going to the bathroom, had told him to watch his little brother
Now the train pulled into a station, and he tried to read the name of it in the glare of the setting sun
He could recognize only two of the four characters: hill and city
Their stop was the next one, but as people got off the train, others were already standing up, reaching for their luggage
The top rolled from the tray table onto the floor, bounced, and slid under the rows in front of him
He crawled on the floor, dodging people’s shoes and thighs and suitcases, until he snatched it back into the safety of his small, warm fist
When he crawled back to his seat, Dudu was gone
She held Dudu the way their mother held him
Dudu, whose head rested on her shoulder, opened his eyes drowsily as she carried him off the train
In an instant they were swarmed by bodies on the platform
Through the window he caught a glimpse of the woman’s face, which looked ordinary, which he’d later fail to describe with any specificity to the sketch artist at the police station
Over the woman’s shoulder, Dudu’s face pinched in confusion
Inside the train, he heard a wail, sharp and alarmed, coming from his own throat
After his brother was abducted on the train between Changsha and Guangzhou, his parents bankrupted themselves
They camped outside the local police station
When the police moved on to other things, they spent all their money on an incompetent local detective
They spent all their time plastering ads on the telephone poles of a city that had been neither a home nor a destination
A few seasons passed before they finally returned to their run-down apartment in Changsha, but it felt like years
His father’s cheeks sagged permanently, as if they were trying to run away from the rest of his face
The room he had once shared with Dudu was frighteningly quiet at night without the sound of Dudu’s soft, wet snores
Back then he believed that the walkie-talkie his father had given him for his seventh birthday had magic powers
At night, he’d take the cold block in his hands and press it against his ear, whispering, “Dudu, Dudu, can you hear me? Come back, I need you for our mission
Over.” Silence spread through the house and wrapped everyone in their own impenetrable cocoon

He knew that his mother blamed him for what had happened, though she never said it aloud, and though he’d told the police that on the train he’d begun screaming and pounding the window right away to get the other passengers’ attention
Some mornings, in the apartment’s heavy stillness, his mother set down boiled eggs in front of him without cooling them in water
They blistered his fingers when he tried to peel them
He knew that she did it on purpose—she used to always cool them for him first
He knew that his father, though he never said it aloud, blamed his mother for what had happened
His father had once swept the hair that his mother would shed in the bathroom without complaint
Now he hardly spent time in the apartment at all
His mother’s white strands piled around the toilet like a thin layer of frost

title: Mike Johnson Will Tend To Your Lawn Now
excerpt: “Heaven forbid, if we lose this majority or whatever, I don’t know what my next chapter of life is, I’m just open to it
body: “Heaven forbid, if we lose this majority or whatever, I don’t know what my next chapter of life is, I’m just open to it
And if God moves on our hearts and says we should, you know, go back to my hometown of Shreveport and start a lawn business, I’ll do that with equal fervor

I mean, I just want to be of my highest and best use to God and to my country.” — Mike Johnson, to Fox News’s Aishah Hasnie Mike Johnson finished his circuit of the lawn on his riding mower, dismounted, and stared at the tree
Yet something about the branches was wrong
But what? If only he could ask Donald Trump for advice! No—this was his new job, his lawn-care business
It was going to be a lot more work than he had anticipated
There should be more jobs like speaker of the House, without any major responsibilities except to sit at the feet of the president and gaze at him in silent adoration
Now Johnson felt like he was working all the time
And, worse, he had to direct his own activities
But after losing the majority, he had been left with no choice
He could not seek election to the minority leadership
The lawns of Shreveport needed him, and he would answer
The biggest question had been what to call the business
Finally, he decided on Mike Johnson Total Landscaping, an homage to his former patron
It was hard to figure out how to begin without Trump’s guiding hand
He knew some things about Trump’s attitude toward lawns, but not all
To cut down 400 trees as quickly as possible was a great act
Pools were generally good—some, but not others
He had made notes of all of this, but there were still so many blanks to fill in
Were grassroots movements good or bad? How could you tell if something was a weed? It was hard to think for himself after so many months out of practice
Occasionally he thought of the time when he had been speaker of the House
What a strange time! It almost felt like a dream

He had understood that the speaker of the House was third in line to the presidency, and therefore it behooved him to remain in careful seclusion from any kind of disturbing news , so that if he were called upon to serve, he would be rested and ready
Yet people were always asking him frustrating questions, as though he were meant to be keeping up on things, approving or disapproving of events, or even taking an active role in them
But he had known better: His purpose was to serve the president
Such a funny title, given that! “Speaker of the House.” He wondered what house it was
Since leaving that role, he’d had much more time to catch up on news
Astounding how much had happened in the country since he left Shreveport! He had been wondering why he saw so few other landscapers
He heard from his friends at Greenwater Services that there had been some roving gangs of masked men making people frightened to leave home
He also heard that there was a war of some kind? Gasoline was certainly expensive, but he had to keep his mower running somehow
Now that he had finally caught up on all the news, he’d started listening to a book on tape: the U.S
What he’d learned disturbed him. “Did you know about this?” he had asked his wife, at the end of his first day trimming hedges. “What?” “Apparently, there are three equal branches of government
Congress is actually the first one mentioned
Equal branches.” “What do you think it means?” she said

He’d kept listening. “Did you know?” he said, the next afternoon. “The leader of that equal branch of government—do you know what that job is called?” She shook her head. “The speaker of the House,” he said. “Isn’t that funny?” She frowned. “But that’s the same name as your old job,” she said
Something was the matter with its branches, but he did not know what to do to fix it
Cut the strong one? Cut the weak one, maybe? If only Donald Trump were here

title: Americans Are Spending Less Time With Friends

body: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight
Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning
What does your ideal night look like? Maybe it’s dinner with friends or a quiet evening at home with family or a partner
If you picked the latter option, you are part of a growing contingent of Americans who are spending less time with friends and, by some measures, more time with family
Although enjoying the company of loved ones can be deeply fulfilling, something may be lost when our household makes up the majority of our social life
In a recent Atlantic story, my colleague Faith Hill explores why friendship is taking a back seat to family time

In one survey, nearly 40 percent of respondents who said they wished they saw friends more cited a lack of money as an obstacle; others pointed to busy schedules and exhaustion. “More Americans are hanging out with family—by choice, but also by necessity,” Faith writes
Friendships offer a type of companionship that family life can’t always provide
But unlike family ties, friendships depend on our continued attention to nurture them, making them meaningful—and easier to lose

title: What Happened to JetBlue?
excerpt: For airlines in the United States, going bankrupt is practically a rite of passage
body: For airlines in the United States, going bankrupt is practically a rite of passage
Since the airline industry was deregulated almost 50 years ago, dozens of airlines have filed for Chapter 11, including each of the so-called Big Three carriers—United, American, and Delta
A notable exception has been JetBlue, which until recently was one of the industry’s few success stories

But after The Wall Street Journal reported last month that the airline’s mounting debt obligations moved senior creditors to hire restructuring advisers, some investors began assuming that bankruptcy was on the way
JetBlue’s CEO, Joanna Geraghty, insists otherwise

On the company’s most recent earnings call, in late October, she at least temporarily assuaged investor anxieties with claims that the airline was not at risk of going under, and was on track to return to profitability next year
Even so, JetBlue is undoubtedly struggling
The carrier has lost more than $3 billion since 2019, the last year it turned a full-year profit, and its debt load has risen swiftly to about $8.4 billion
The proximate cause of the company’s current woes is obvious: Fuel costs have soared since the Iran war began
But the challenge the company faces is more fundamental than that

JetBlue has been struggling because it finds itself in what’s sometimes called the “mushy middle,” caught between discount airlines on the low end and the big legacy carriers, which have lots of expense-account-wielding business travelers and lucrative transatlantic routes, on the high end. [ Read: An SNL sketch to make airlines feel ashamed ] When JetBlue began flying, in 2000, being in between was a strength: The company explicitly positioned itself as a stylish and plucky alternative to the ultra-low-cost carriers and the legacy carriers
It offered more legroom, good snacks, free satellite television, and leather seats to every customer, but still managed to be significantly cheaper than the big airlines
It was able to pull this off because its jet fleet was made up of only one type of plane, which kept maintenance costs down, and its workforce was not unionized

The carrier also initially offered just one class of seat, which helped it maximize space, even with the extra legroom.JetBlue’s marketing leaned into the idea that the company offered a new model for the industry, promising to “bring humanity back to air travel.” The carrier was so successful so quickly that legacy airlines tried to adopt this model for themselves: Delta and United started lower-cost, would-be JetBlue competitors in the 2000s, but both quickly failed

Meanwhile, JetBlue expanded its relatively low-cost, high-value offerings; in 2014, it launched a premium cabin for transcontinental routes called Mint, featuring lie-flat seats and fares well below those of the big carriers
By the late 2010s, it was the fifth-biggest airline in the country
Over much of the past decade, though, that sweet spot in the market that JetBlue had made its own has shrunk
On the low end, new discount airlines have sprung up, offering no frills but also very cheap fares

On the higher end, the legacy carriers have gotten better at exploiting their lucrative revenue sources, jacking up prices on business travel and transatlantic routes, and using their giant customer bases to partner with credit-card companies willing to pay them billions
Even if the carrier had wanted to slash prices to compete with the discounters, its costs are now far too high for it to do so

Those jets that were brand-new when the company launched are aging, driving up maintenance costs, and its workforce began unionizing in 2014, driving up labor costs. (It also does not want to give up on the premium amenities that have made it so distinctive.) At the same time, JetBlue has struggled to compete with the legacy carriers for more profitable business travelers because most of its planes lack business- or first-class cabins, and the company doesn’t fly to nearly as many cities as the legacy carriers do
Nor has it been able to leverage its loyalty program, TrueBlue, the way the big carriers have leveraged theirs

TrueBlue will generate about $1 billion in revenue for the airline this year, which seems impressive until you realize that Delta makes more than $8 billion annually from the SkyMiles credit cards issued by American Express. [ Read: The only thing worse than Spirit Airlines ] These problems are in some respects specific to the airline industry
But JetBlue’s troubles are also emblematic of a basic fact about American business, which is that it has simply become harder for companies targeting the middle of the market to succeed

Traditional department stores such as Macy’s and Kohl’s have found themselves squeezed between big-box retailers and e-tailers such as Walmart, Target, and Amazon on the low end and premium retailers on the high end
Casual sit-down restaurants including Applebee’s and TGI Fridays have gotten edged out by fast-casual restaurants and fine dining

The disappearance of the American-made passenger car is also part of this story: Cars such as the Chrysler Sebring and the Chevy Malibu weren’t cheap enough, relative to their perceived level of quality, to compete with the perennially reliable Toyota Camry and Honda Accord, but they also weren’t fancy enough to compete with Lexus and Tesla
Consumers have become more price-conscious and are better informed about quality and cachet
So offering a pretty-good option at an almost-premium price doesn’t cut it anymore

It still has valuable assets, including most notably its brand, which remains surprisingly strong—even if it’s now doing many of the things that annoy people about traditional airlines, such as raising baggage fees
Its planes still have more legroom and free Wi-Fi
And next month, the carrier is going to be rolling out first-class cabins on many of its domestic routes, which should boost revenue
When fuel costs come down, the company may well turn a profit again
But being JetBlue is never going to be easy
It’s stuck in the middle, and these days, that’s the toughest place for a business to be.

title: ICE After the Blowout
excerpt: “D eportations will continue,” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote in a post on X the day after voters punished his party in the mi
body: “D eportations will continue,” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote in a post on X the day after voters punished his party in the midterm election
The three-word statement appeared to be aimed at quieting an incipient debate among Republicans over whether President Trump should ease his ICE crackdown

Two years after he won back the White House promising the largest mass-deportation campaign in U.S. history, Trump and his party suffered monumental losses in states such as Texas, Georgia, and North Carolina, where voters—especially Hispanics—swung hard to Democrats
More moderate Republicans have urged the administration to adopt a quieter enforcement approach, focusing more narrowly on criminal offenders

Although the president has reportedly expressed concern to those close to him that some ICE tactics have gone too far, he has not ordered specific policy changes, according to three senior officials I spoke with at DHS
Those officials and others I’ve talked with told me they aren’t expecting a pullback, either
Trump’s decision to name Stephen Miller as his chief of staff yesterday places the chief architect and principal ideologue of the ICE campaign in charge of his administration
Miller’s promotion will give him even more power to mobilize other federal agencies to help ICE maximize deportations
Since Trump’s return to the White House, Republicans in Congress have given the administration nearly a quarter of a trillion dollars for the crackdown, aiming for 1 million deportations a year
ICE has obtained upwards of $110 billion, more than 11 times its annual budget, and the funding surge has created a powerful inertia

Absent a major policy reversal from Trump or a successful intervention by Democratic majorities in Congress—a long shot, experts say—Trump’s mass-deportation campaign will continue with its mandate to add more officers, more deportation flights, and more immigration jails
The campaign includes handing out wads of cash to local police and sheriff departments, which help the agency boost arrests

Prior to the midterms, ICE launched a hiring push to add 5,000 more employees—mostly deportation officers—by the end of the year. “Regardless of the political pressures that the White House may be feeling on immigration enforcement, the money creates a huge amount of momentum on its own,” Sarah Pierce, an immigration policy expert at the center-left think tank Third Way, told me

ICE has so much money that it will have to double its rate of spending to use it all before its deadline at the end of the 2029 fiscal year, she said. “Pulling that back would be extremely difficult for the White House.” [ Read: Losing the ‘big-ass truck’ vote ] Despite the midterm results, there hasn’t been a broad consensus in the Republican Party that overzealous ICE tactics were a vulnerability, and some right-wing commentators have pointed to exit-poll data showing that immigration was the top motivating issue for Republican voter turnout

At a polling place in the Dallas suburbs where I spoke with voters on Tuesday, several of the Republican supporters I met said they wanted Trump to stay the course. “Gotta keep locking it down,” said Danny, a 32-year-old hospital staffer I met outside a public library in Plano, north of Dallas
Danny told me he didn’t want his last name published, because he worried that he’d be harassed

His hometown and surrounding Collin County were reliably Republican when he was growing up, he said, but the region’s economic boom had brought in more transplants. “They keep voting for Democrats,” he said. “Democrats vote for more immigration
It’s a vicious cycle.” James Talarico, the Democratic winner of the Senate race in Texas, won Collin County by 12 points on Tuesday, a 23-point swing from Trump’s 2024 victory
It was the first time this century that Democrats have won statewide races in the county
Trump won nearly half the Hispanic vote nationwide in 2024, but this year Hispanics are estimated to have voted for Democrats by a 69–29 percent margin

C ould Democrats use their large majorities in Congress next year to force the administration to rein in ICE? Claire Trickler-McNulty, an attorney who has held several high-ranking roles at ICE, most recently during the Biden administration, told me that it will be hard for Democrats to change the trajectory of ICE spending

If Democrats pass an appropriations bill with language constraining or shifting ICE funds, Trump would have to sign it. “I don’t have a lot of confidence that he would sign that, but people I’ve talked to on the Hill feel like there may be a window or a path to a clawback, if you combine that with something he cares about,” Trickler-McNulty said

Trump has said he doesn’t want to spend the next two years “vetoing everything,” although the White House has also circulated a photo of a red VETO hat sitting on the Resolute Desk with the president in the background

Trump told Politico late Tuesday night that he’d be willing to work with Democrats on immigration reform if it were “appropriate and good for the country.” But the possibility of such negotiations could reduce the likelihood that Trump orders a different tack for ICE in the meantime

Mark Krikorian, the executive director of the Center for Immigration Studies, a leading immigration-restrictionist group, told me that the Trump administration has already shifted tactics, and could do so again

After the killings of two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis in January, Trump demoted Greg Bovino , the performative Border Patrol commander who was leading the crackdown in the city, and replaced Kristi Noem with Mullin, who said he wanted a more low-key ICE approach
That change marked the end of what Krikorian described as “theatricality,” generating ready-for-TV images of masked federal forces staging operations that thrilled the president’s base

But Krikorian said that an “imbalance” remains between “body-armor enforcement versus briefcase enforcement.” Trump could direct ICE to conduct more enforcement at worksites—not necessarily with raids that would send people running, Krikorian said, but with mundane audits that check Social Security numbers and other documents. “Worksite enforcement is something that has been very much lacking in this administration,” he said

It’s a lot less photogenic and a lot less politically tumultuous to just send in some bureaucrats.” [ Read: The secretary of homeland ] ICE continued to ramp up, with less fanfare, after Minneapolis , and the agency is now making more than 50,000 arrests a month, its highest rate ever
Officers have achieved those levels in part by using automated technologies, such as license-plate readers, and powerful database tools to make more traffic stops
Those public encounters deepened the backlash to ICE over the summer when officers shot several unarmed immigrants—two fatally—as they attempted to drive away
City and state governments have joined in that backlash, a trend that could accelerate with the widespread Democratic victories this week
The mayor of Houston announced yesterday that the city’s police will no longer contact ICE about nonviolent offenders who lack legal status

White-collar enforcement would not necessarily lead to arrests and deportations, but it would make it more likely for immigrants who are in the United States illegally to leave on their own, Krikorian said
The frustrations that Trump has been hearing from business owners may weigh against a crackdown on employers
Vice President Vance, who is considering running for president in 2028, appeared to signal a preference for that approach on Wednesday in a lengthy X post that assessed the party’s defeat

Vance wrote that he was “open” to shifting ICE’s focus to businesses that “hire illegal labor,” but said he didn’t support “amnesty,” the catch-all term used by immigration hard-liners who oppose creating a path to legal status for the estimated 12 million to 15 million immigrants who are illegally present in the United States. “Anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you,” Vance wrote
Pierce told me that she interpreted Vance’s post as a defense of the administration’s crackdown that was aimed at Republicans who view the midterm results as a rebuke

She said she’ll be watching to see if pressure on the administration to change tactics builds in the coming weeks or if the White House remains defensive and determined to follow the same course. [ Read: Repudiation ] There were also signs in Vance’s post of the conundrum that he and other potential Republican presidential candidates will likely face if they try to succeed Trump

Although there is broad support across the electorate for the deportation of immigrants who commit violent crimes or pose a threat to public safety, those immigrants represent only 10 to 20 percent of ICE arrests

title: How Democrats can make good on their new mandate
excerpt: Wes Moore is often mentioned as a potential Democratic presidential candidate in 2028, speculation that he has not exactly batted down. | Monica Morgan/Getty Im
body: Wes Moore is often mentioned as a potential Democratic presidential candidate in 2028, speculation that he has not exactly batted down. | Monica Morgan/Getty Images The midterm elections were great for Democrats everywhere, but some triumphed even more decisively than others: Maryland Gov
Wes Moore, for example, cruised to reelection with roughly 63 percent of the vote

Voters pushed Republicans out — and kept Democrats like Moore in power — in part because of their concerns over a handful of critical issues, including the rising cost of living, the Iran war, and the growing dominance of AI and data centers

The question now is how Democrats can best wield their new power to act on the currents that carried them into office.  For Moore, the stakes may be particularly high: He’s often mentioned as a potential Democratic presidential candidate in 2028, speculation that he has not exactly batted down
America, Actually host Astead Herndon spoke with Moore about his vision for how the Democrats should proceed
As Moore put it, this is a moment in which the party will have to move quickly on the problems that motivate voters most.  Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel
Lowering cost is the top priority for voters, and, frankly, it was where they penalized Trump the most
What’s the single biggest thing Democrats could do to address folks’ cost of living concerns? Actually move fast to fix the things

For example, in Maryland, we’ve done permitting reform to be able to speed up affordable housing, right? And I did not need a 10-year research paper to tell me that we have an issue with affordable housing
If it’s state-owned land, don’t tell me why we can’t do something

The reason we made the largest investments in childcare in our state’s history is because it is insane when you’re watching the fact that people are spending thirty and forty percent of their paychecks on child care and knowing how much that’s actually going to impact [them]
So there are things that we can do right now to be able to address it.  But I also think that there are things that we need Washington to be able to do
For example, gas prices: There’s no governor that can impact gas prices
We just need to stop fighting stupid wars
There’s no governor that is impacting national energy policy or national grocery prices
What we need to do is stop allowing illegal tariff policy to happen
So I do think that there are things that Washington Democrats have got to do, and that they need to move fast on
But I also think that we don’t need to wait for them to be able to put things in place that we know that actually work
I wonder what universal healthcare means to you
Is that the government providing insurance? If you look at what we’ve done here in Maryland, we’ve been able to actually come up with platforms through our Total Cost of Care [Model]
We’re actually working with our hospitals
Our hospitals have a universal budget, and are then able to make sure that people are getting the care that they need
That has done a tremendous job of being able to help to break the cost curve
Maryland is one of the only states in the country where you’re watching the cost of healthcare actually go down, [while] also being able to increase coverage
A lot of the Democrats’ affordability message came out of Mamdani’s win
I remember him telling me the one thing he would never budge on is the belief that billionaires shouldn’t exist
Do you think billionaires should exist? I lose no sleep over the amount of billionaires in our society
I do lose sleep over the amount of children that are growing up in poverty
And I think those who [do] have, have a responsibility to support and uplift and create pathways for those who do not
Here in our state, we actually cut taxes for the middle class

And I said [to wealthy Marylanders], you need to invest more to make sure that we’re doing things like we’re doing: having the fastest public safety turnaround story in the United States of America, having math and reading scores in our public schools now at five-year highs
And I did ask wealthy Marylanders to invest a little bit more to make sure we can get those kinds of results
You served in Afghanistan and are a veteran

When we think about this incoming Democratic Congress, should they continue funding a war that Americans have mostly found is not in their interest? No, and they shouldn’t have funded in the first place.  I’ve heard the argument that that leaves soldiers behind
No, because we’re talking about a president who unilaterally went to war without even asking Congress for authority
The president does not have the authority to just wage war by himself
That is something that the Constitution lays out
Congress is the only one that has the authority for that

And truthfully, this Congress has been so caught up in the aura of the president of the United States that they have not been leaders; they have been cheerleaders.  Part of the issue is that this Congress needs to be held to account, and that’s exactly what I think happened on Tuesday

title: You’re going to hate shopping in an AI economy
excerpt: When was the last time you had to call customer support with a problem? Can you remember how it went?  If you’re like most Americans, the answer is “probab
body: When was the last time you had to call customer support with a problem? Can you remember how it went?  If you’re like most Americans, the answer is “probably not very well.” And that may be understating it: As of 2025, according to the “ National Customer Rage Survey ” — yes, it’s a real thing — nearly 80 percent of Americans ran into a “product or service problem” in the past year, and nearly two-thirds experienced “rage” in attempting to resolve it

We have, in short, entered into a rage economy, where high prices and inflation have made everyday products unaffordable at the same time as our experiences buying those products have filled us with fury

The landscape isn’t really improving, either: As a consumer, you’re faced with terrible customer service, unhelpful chatbots, and products that are worse than they used to be .  If you listen to the big AI companies, however, there’s a light on the horizon: AI agents , which can step in and do the things you don’t want to (like waiting on hold or dueling it out with aforementioned unhelpful chatbots)

But are AI agents really the key to fixing our rage economy? Or will they just be what brings it deeper into chaos? Charlie Warzel , a staff writer at The Atlantic, recently went deep on what happens when we bring AI agents into our already contentious consumer experience (along with his colleague Matteo Wong)

Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with Warzel about how AI agents are being used for the grating parts of our lives, what happens when companies use their own AI agents to deal with consumers, and where this all might leave us.  Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
Charlie, we spoke about how the economy and how customer service works is making everyone rage out
Are AI agents going to make it better or worse? In the early time, it’s probably going to make it a lot worse

What we are essentially seeing right now is that these agents are inundating the internet with persistence.  These are relentless things that are tasked to do the onerous activities that we don’t want to do
And they’re already flooding call centers
They’re flooding restaurant reservations
They’re flooding plumbers and people who run small businesses with requests and queries
And they’re not people.  It’s going to make a lot of people feel, honestly, pretty awful
The world has all of a sudden become very inhuman or there are these inhuman burdens being put on the humans who don’t have agents yet to work on their behalf
And that imbalance is going to make a lot of people pretty mad
You wrote for The Atlantic that we are not ready for our coming AI agent future

How are we not ready for this? If it reaches a critical mass, the argument is that we aren’t ready for it because the economy is built off of, and in a lot of ways thrives off of, inefficiency — off of the fact that people aren’t paying perfect attention to everything.  People aren’t moving their money from savings account to savings account every day because they’re getting the margins on a slightly better interest rate or something like that
This entire subscription economy is based off of inefficiency

You don’t cancel the thing that you don’t use for a long period of time or it lays dormant for a while.  But what these AI agents offer in their most idealized fashion is that they pay perfect attention to everything, all the time
They are hypervigilant and able to act on your behalf in inhuman ways

And if a large portion of the population is using these to do their banking, to do their e-commerce, and at the same time you have these large organizations like banks, healthcare companies, platforms like Amazon and Walmart, you’re going to see just incredible amounts of chaos.  The economy would, in that way, start to behave more like the stock market, where prices fluctuate on the order of milliseconds
And from watching the stock market over decades, I don’t know if we want diapers to behave like securities
One of the more speculative but also illustrative ideas here is what people refer to as an agentic bank run

This is the idea that, say, 5 million people are using the same agent to do all of their banking and they all identify at the same time that there is a high-yield savings account that everyone should be in
So they move money en masse: millions of agents pulling money out of one account to the next, and then those banks are struggling because they’ve just lost all of these deposits at once
It’s theoretically possible that something like that could happen all of the time
Is this a two-way street? Are the companies also adopting agents into every part of their processes and consumer relations? Yes
It’s slower on that end, but I like to think of this as an arms race.  A lot of retailers, especially Amazon, have blocked a number of these agents from accessing their platform

Because even though Amazon can make good money off of these sales, they don’t yet want these companies to have access to their backend infrastructure.  There are a lot of corporate secrets like inventory and who’s buying what and who’s selling what

These agents can act as really good intelligence gatherers if they’re granted access to these platforms.  What you’ll see eventually is that the retailers are going to have demands: “You guys can let the agents on the platform, but you can’t undercut our prices in this way.” It will just be something that you have to trust that your AI agent company is making a deal in your best interest

I think that that’s really interesting because you could end up having this future where everything feels really good as a consumer because it’s frictionless: “My agent’s going to do all this stuff for me while I sleep or while I’m hanging out with my family or whatnot.” And in reality, what’s going to happen is you’re just having someone do something for you, but nothing else has really changed
It’s not that much more helpful to you because these companies have taken care of themselves first

That is what Sam Altman and Mark Zuckerberg are trying to sell us.  Do you think it’s a pipe dream or do you think there is some reality, one day, when we as a society will say, “This consumer-facing AI agent world of ours is better than the one we had a hundred years ago”? Something that I think is really funny is Meta, with Muse, has really dominated the conversation about these AI assistants
And this is the company that wanted to connect the world, that says that us being together is this universal good, it is strengthening the bonds of humanity
This is a tool that is fundamentally antisocial
You don’t have to interact with those people if you don’t want to

I’m not trying to romanticize running really annoying errands when you’re busy and your kids are sick and you’ve got work deadlines and things, but there’s also the experience of interacting with people on a day-to-day basis that is foundational to our humanity and these things basically want to automate that away.  That’s a real thing that we need to think about and grapple with
And the other part of this is, what are we freeing this time up for? I’m always wondering that myself, because that’s what they keep promising
You’re going to have so much time…to do what? To then just spend more time scrolling your platforms? To spend more time scrolling your platforms, spend more time working

There is a lack of thought about what a human is for if we fully embrace automation in all these different ways, right? It’s one thing to say, “I wish it was easier to buy paper towels on Amazon.” It’s another to say— It’s pretty easy, though

title: This election’s biggest AI story isn’t about data centers
excerpt: Abdul El-Sayed, then-Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, speaks during a news conference near the construction site of "The Barn" data center, developed
body: Abdul El-Sayed, then-Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, speaks during a news conference near the construction site of "The Barn" data center, developed by Related Digital for Oracle and OpenAI, in Saline Township, Michigan, on July 30, 2026. | Sarah Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images You’ve probably been hearing a lot about data centers this week.  Candidates in several races made regulating data centers a key part of their campaigns
Now, 40 ballot measures to slow or stop data centers have passed

And in an exit poll , when respondents were asked how important AI and data centers were in their vote for Congress, 56 percent answered that it was a “crucial or a major factor.”  Data centers are the physical infrastructure that powers AI, and they’ve become deeply unpopular not just because of their noisiness, ugliness, or electricity demand , but because of what they symbolize: the acceleration of a technology that many Americans fear and that they feel Silicon Valley is foisting upon them.   Key takeaways Key figures to watch include Abdul El-Sayed, Jon Ossoff, and Scott Wiener
Maria Cantwell has already put out a framework that could have bipartisan appeal
Data centers have grabbed the headlines, but the bigger story is the sweeping success of candidates who prioritize AI safety
These leaders will be poised to rein in the tech itself through hearings and lawmaking

If you’re one of the Americans worried about AI — or just prefer a more serious regulatory approach over the hands-off, Trump White House approach — there’s a problem with confining your attention to data centers
Even a successful push against them won’t address the bigger issues around the technology
And picking off data center projects one by one will slow, but not stop, the buildout
AI companies will still find jurisdictions that are willing to let them build — it’ll just cost them more
The election outcome that matters far more, though it was far less trumpeted, is that voters just elected a new crop of leaders promising to actually push to regulate the tech itself
These are people who are concerned not just about AI’s physical infrastructure, but about AI regulation and safety

And they’ve signaled that they’ll push for laws that address the full spectrum of risks from AI — from cyber hacks and job losses all the way to bioweapons, power concentration, and even the possibility of human extinction.  In fact, for AI watchers, one of the most striking things about this election cycle is how safety-pilled many candidates have become since the major AI hacks this summer. “If you go back before the summer, most conversations from policymakers around AI were at a very, very high level of abstraction

Few of them were focused on how these AI models may be highly capable and may pose rather unique risks,” Mackenzie Arnold, an analyst at the Institute for Law & AI, told me. “But there’s been a big shift.”  The midterm results — and the Democrats’ stunning takeover of Congress — improve the odds of reining in AI

But now, the big question is: Can the new victors use the momentum they built up around data centers — the kitchen-table issue that initially brought many voters into the tent — and broaden out beyond that to mobilize for greater AI safety? They may have a lot of ideas, but are they any good? The new (and newly emboldened) crop of AI safety advocates  Among the newly elected Democrats, a striking number are very vocal about AI risks
And a few have clearly taken the time to educate themselves on the finer points

So before considering what concrete changes they can actually implement, it’s worth getting to know what they’ve proposed.  Abdul El-Sayed , who won the Michigan Senate race, said that we need a “full-on pause” on frontier AI research
He’s also advocated for global coordination on a slowdown, including a treaty with China aimed at avoiding an arms race dynamic
He supports a ban on recursive self-improvement, where AI models build the next, even smarter AI models
He also wants a new federal safety agency that would inspect companies and block releases if necessary

Even if not all his ideas resonate with experts (like the simplistic idea of a “kill switch” for dangerous models), having him in the Senate means that AI safety advocates will have an easier time arguing for a pause on frontier research.  Another winner to watch is Jon Ossoff , who prevailed in his Georgia Senate race

In his victory speech, he lambasted AI developers, saying, “The titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction.”  Back in September, he impressed safety advocates by explicitly mentioning “catastrophic risks” like AI-engineered bioweapons

Conveying his priorities, he said , “A capable president would move swiftly to secure and reassure the American people, rush inspectors into frontier labs, fortify the nation against bioterrorism, demand legislation from Congress, and lead the world toward an AI treaty
But President Trump is compromised.”  Two other Democrats with strong AI safety bona fides and specific policy ideas have emerged victorious this week

Scott Wiener — the longtime California state senator who was behind two important pieces of legislation, SB 1047 (which was ultimately vetoed ) and SB 53 (which was signed into law) — won Nancy Pelosi’s seat this week

He’s said he’ll work to institute strict federal safety standards and “guard against catastrophic risk from AI.”  And Manny Rutinel — who cosponsored a 2024 law that sought to regulate AI use — won his race in Colorado

Rutinel has ties to effective altruism, a movement long preoccupied with AI safety, and you can hear it in the way he talks: “This technology has a 10 percent risk of wiping out human civilization,” he recently told The New York Times. “I don’t want human civilization to come to an end.” Sam Forstag, who just became Montana’s first Democratic member of Congress in decades, also stated that AI poses an “existential risk to all of humanity.” Troy Jackson, the Democrat who won his Senate race in Maine, has vowed that he’s “not going to let the billionaires write the rules,” adding , “We are not that far from ‘Terminator,’ and I don’t want to be ‘hasta la vista, baby.’”  You can expect these new victors to be reliable votes supporting the cause of AI regulation come early 2027

But what, exactly, might that look like? What Democrats plan to do now on AI As Democrats are poised to take power in Congress, they will have two big levers to pull on AI safety: hearings and lawmaking.  Now that the election is over, expect a whole lot of hearings

Ed Markey, who won reelection in Massachusetts, signaled that he’s coming for Big Tech executives. “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” he posted on X

What will it look like if these executives are called to testify under oath? “Some of the hearings are going to be focused on safety practices — and evidence that the company’s practices are not up to snuff,” Arnold told me. “Asking for answers to questions of:  ‘Why didn’t you find that earlier? Why didn’t you tell us?’ And while that doesn’t get you all the way [to safety], this public pressure is why so many companies have adopted voluntary practices, why they’ve improved their internal monitoring, their incident reporting, their response time to various incidents.” As for lawmaking, experts I spoke with are now bullish that we’ll see much stronger AI legislation in 2027 than we’ve seen to date
Maria Cantwell, who’s slated to chair the Senate Commerce Committee, is a key player to watch
She’s already put out a framework for governing AI that could have bipartisan appeal, which she’s called a precursor to legislation

It requires mandatory safety standards for cutting-edge AI models, independent testing and audits that models would have to pass before release, and prompt reporting of safety incidents. “Cantwell is going to push that, and she’s in a place to basically be the voice of the caucus on that,” Brad Carson, an advocate for stricter AI policies who leads Americans for Responsible AI and a former congressman, told me. “Every single Democrat supports it, and all they need is five or six Republicans to beat the filibuster, and I bet you they can find that.” Carson is hopeful that Democrats can get Republican votes “especially as the gravitational pull of the White House eases,” he said. “Trump has led them down the primrose path of defeat
A lot of smart politicians are going to be distancing themselves.” Yes, President Donald Trump ultimately holds veto power
And he’s allowed American tech companies to race ahead on the technology with very few guardrails

But as AI companies make more and more concessions to safety in light of security incidents, the president may be more willing to sign on to some safety regulations.  “He’s mercurial enough that I can see him signing something like this,” Carson told me, “especially if some of these Republicans say, ‘Look, we’re getting battered on data centers and AI
Let’s do this.’” Of course, the most surefire way to gain control of AI lawmaking, unobstructed by a veto, would be to lay the groundwork for a Democratic White House in 2028

And the midterms showed that a focus on reining in AI can help propel Democrats to victory. “The road to 2028 starts today,” wrote Alex Bores , the New York Assembly member who has made AI his main focus. “In order to maintain voters’ trust and avoid catastrophic risk, we need a unified baseline around AI safety in the Democratic Party.” Although many voters focused on data centers this election cycle, it’s reasonable to predict — as cyber breaches and other security incidents proliferate — that they will move from symbol to substance, focusing more on safety in the run-up to 2028.    “We shouldn’t view voter sentiment towards data centers and AI as stagnant or static,” Arnold told me. “I think it will continue to update to events in the world, and I think it will increasingly focus on AI itself as we see events in the world that make that very obvious to people.” Or as Greg Casar, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus that sets policy and legislative strategy, put it , “The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election, and in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics.” The savviest politicians are already preparing with that earthquake in mind.

title: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
excerpt: A robot cleaned my apartment for $30 — San Francisco startup Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots into people's homes, piloted remotely by humans who co
body: A robot cleaned my apartment for $30 — San Francisco startup Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots into people's homes, piloted remotely by humans who collect training data while the robots clean — making the service cheaper than you'd expect for something this futuristic
Cute but clumsy — The four-and-a-half-foot robot climbed stairs like it was drunk, knocked over olive oil, and left taps dripping — but impressively reattached its toilet brush wand three times

The Jetsons, with caveats — If autonomous cleaning robots become real, the human cost could be steep: cleaning workers could lose their jobs, and U.S. policy is nowhere near ready to handle that. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148090" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner
I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser
But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist
I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons , even if just for an hour
I was also motivated by journalistic interest
In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up

Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists
As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants
Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round
Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product
At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit
But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain

They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.  But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute

Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks)
Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors
With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos

Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them
These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data
Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there

But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help

If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide
The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle
It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee
That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door
I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps
Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing

When I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she said
Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps

As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment

Without remote assistance, the robot couldn’t clean, and so it, and Weinzierl, departed before my booked hour was up. (Back in September, Weinzierl or another Tau representative remained with the robot throughout its visit, but she says that’s no longer necessary.) You can’t fault Tau on customer service, though
Weinzierl quickly emailed me to apologize, comp the visit, and offer me another on the house (minus whatever price I assign to my data privacy)—and that was all before I told her I was a journalist

I scheduled the next cleaning for about a month later, after a couple of trips out of town, and it went much more smoothly—the robot got up my stairs without much assistance, though still with the drunken stagger
In the hour it was there, it did a creditable job of cleaning my kitchen (though it didn’t brave the stove) and even saved me my most dreaded cleaning task, the toilet

That was its most impressive performance: Three times the head fell off its toilet cleaning wand, and three times it managed to reattach it by poking around with the handle until it made contact at just the right angle
The robot is still rough around the edges, which is to be expected for a product in beta
It repeatedly left my taps dripping, it knocked over a (closed) bottle of olive oil, and it couldn’t manage to right an air purifier that it had toppled
But I easily forgave all those missteps because of how charming it was
As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out

<title>Pope Leo’s trip is a homecoming to Peru – where debate over liberation theology roiled the church during his early years as a priest</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770403/original/file-20261105-64-909jxl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7102%2C4734&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A mototaxi drives past a banner of Pope Leo XIV in Chiclayo, Peru, on Nov. 5, 2026, ahead of his trip to Latin America.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/PeruPope/7296c0075d304da7a2ef4351555684f7/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=pope%20leo&amp;currentItemNo=2&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Martin Mejia</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Pope Leo XIV travels to Latin America on Nov. 6, 2026, with <a href="https://press.vatican.va/content/salastampa/it/bollettino/pubblico/2026/09/21/0736/01738.html#en">a packed itinerary</a> that will bring him through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It is Leo’s first trip to the region since his elevation to the papacy – and a homecoming for <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-pope-is-peruvian-how-2-decades-in-south-america-shaped-the-vision-of-pope-leo-xiv-256415">a pope who spent two decades in Peru</a> and holds Peruvian citizenship.</p>

<p>As <a href="https://www.rit.edu/directory/eblgla-eben-levey">a historian</a> of <a href="https://doi.org/10.13016/4bla-77sh">Catholicism in the late 20th century</a>, I couldn’t help but notice that <a href="https://press.vatican.va/content/salastampa/it/bollettino/pubblico/2026/09/21/0736/01738.html">the pope’s plans</a> walk a fine line during a fraught political moment in Latin America.</p>

<p>Leo plans to meet with the <a href="https://en.mercopress.com/2026/11/03/the-pope-arrives-in-an-argentina-where-bishops-are-among-milei-s-firmest-critics">right-wing presidents of Argentina</a> <a href="https://www.ncronline.org/vatican/vatican-news/pope-leos-latin-america-trip-high-stakes-homecoming">and Peru</a>. He will also visit sites often associated with the progressive wing of the Catholic Church, including Casavalle, one of the <a href="https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20261101-seen-and-heard-uruguay-neighborhood-places-hopes-in-pope">poorest neighborhoods</a> in Uruguay’s capital. In Argentina, where President Javier Milei has <a href="https://apnews.com/article/argentina-javier-milei-trump-disabilities-austerity-6d98fb3cecc91fe4f3e3f8800826275e">drastically cut</a> funding for disability services, the pope will go to a Catholic home for disabled people.</p>

<p>And in Chiclayo, Peru, where Leo served as a bishop, he will pray at a chapel dedicated to St. Óscar Romero. A Salvadoran archbishop, Romero <a href="https://www.ucpress.edu/books/assassination-of-a-saint/paper">was assassinated in 1980</a> after years of speaking out against the human rights violations committed by the <a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/36700/the-massacre-at-el-mozote-by-mark-danner/">U.S.-supported</a> <a href="https://www.calmigration.org/learn-chapter/civil-war">Salvadoran military</a>. His ministry was influenced by <a href="https://theconversation.com/after-50-years-liberation-theology-is-still-reshaping-catholicism-and-politics-but-what-is-it-186804">liberation theology</a>, a controversial movement born in Peru that roiled church politics for decades – including during Leo’s years in Peru.</p>

<h2>What is liberation theology?</h2>

<p>The name itself was coined in a 1968 lecture by <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/23/world/americas/gustavo-gutierrez-dead.html">Gustavo Gutiérrez</a>, a Peruvian theologian and priest. He expanded on his ideas in a 1971 book, “<a href="https://orbisbooks.com/products/9781626985414?srsltid=AYCX9vIJkIEBTafm65WkZiA2WWXGZFkSkEwMIPHf0HdvB5Xz2kRYparw">A Theology of Liberation</a>.” </p>

<p>Gutiérrez and like-minded theologians argued that Christians have a moral duty <a href="https://theconversation.com/after-50-years-liberation-theology-is-still-reshaping-catholicism-and-politics-but-what-is-it-186804">to liberate the oppressed</a>. They saw poverty, violence, racism and discrimination as not just problems but collective sins. While building on earlier Catholic social teachings, these “liberationists” envisioned profound change that went beyond the spiritual care and charitable work of traditional Latin American Catholicism. </p>

<p>Catholics <a href="https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/E/bo3631145.html">inspired by liberation theology</a> created community organizations and work cooperatives, organized labor unions and fostered other initiatives that sought to measurably improve the lives of the poor. In <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/liberation-theology-and-the-others-9781793633637/">my own research</a>, I’ve documented how priests and nuns in rural Mexico helped organize transportation, corn milling and carpentry cooperatives.</p>

<p>Gutiérrez also argued that Christians should use Marxist ideas about <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/pedagogy-of-the-oppressed-9781501314131/">analyzing society and the economy</a> to <a href="https://monthlyreview.org/9780853450931/">better understand inequality</a>. In nations like Peru, <a href="https://doi.org/10.4324/9780429315060">which possessed rich natural resources</a>, liberationists tailored their economic justice projects to address how international and national companies profited off the low wages of miners and farmers.</p>

<p>During the Cold War, however, these ideas led some politicians and church leaders to accuse liberationists of socialism and communism.</p>

<p>A minority fringe of liberationists did embrace left-ring radicalism. <a href="https://kellogg.nd.edu/space-utopia-christians-socialism-chile">Christians for Socialism</a>, for example, argued that liberation <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/blog/2025/12/12/the-chilean-christians-for-socialism-movement-liberationist-third-worldist-and-utopian/">meant rejecting capitalism</a>. Some clergy, although only a handful, even <a href="https://www.routledge.com/Camilo-Torres-Priest-Liberation-Theologian-Guerrilla-Fighter/Ginzberg/p/book/9781032990255">picked up arms</a> to fight alongside clandestine left-wing revolutionary groups. </p>

<h2>A wary pope</h2>

<p>This presented a dilemma to the Vatican. </p>

<p>In 1891, Pope Leo XIII – <a href="https://theconversation.com/19th-century-catholic-teachings-21st-century-tech-how-concerns-about-ai-guided-pope-leos-choice-of-name-256645">the current pope’s namesake</a> – <a href="https://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiii/en/encyclicals/documents/hf_l-xiii_enc_15051891_rerum-novarum.html">published “Rerum Novarum</a>,” an encyclical focused on workers’ rights amid the Industrial Revolution. Since then, the Vatican had critiqued the worst excesses of capitalism while also rejecting socialism and communism, which it viewed as godless ideologies. </p>

<p>During the 1960s and ’70s, Pope Paul VI generally <a href="https://www.commonwealmagazine.org/introduction-%E2%80%98commonweal%E2%80%99-and-liberation-theology">supported local initiatives by liberationist Catholics</a>, including some <a href="https://www.nybooks.com/online/2026/05/24/the-education-of-pope-leo-xiv/">in Chulucanas, Peru</a>, where Leo began his missionary work. Paul appointed and elevated bishops who shared a vision that the church could help empower the poor and alleviate oppression. </p>

<p>But the Vatican shifted when the Polish cardinal Karol Józef Wojtyla became Pope John Paul II in 1978. For most of his adult life, Poland had been part of the Soviet bloc, which imposed restrictions on organized religion. A <a href="https://www.anneapplebaum.com/2005/04/06/how-the-pope-defeated-communism/">staunch opponent of communism</a>, <a href="https://time.com/archive/6854086/religion-john-paul-vs-liberation-theology/">he worried about liberation theology’s</a> use of Marxist analysis. So did one of his top Vatican officials, Joseph Ratzinger – the future Pope Benedict XVI.</p>

<p>The Vatican began investigating <a href="https://wipfandstock.com/products/marx-and-the-bible-9781592444854?srsltid=AYCX9vK51gjTntA4LFREX5-quPazIhRZj3zxLHw_WdGvf0hAHqxu3p6B">some liberation theologians</a> for violations of church teachings. In 1985, for example, Brazilian liberationist theologian Leonardo Boff was ordered to observe a <a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/813628776">year of silence</a> – no publishing, no public speaking – to discipline him for his critique of the church’s hierarchy. Several priests <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/world-latin-america-28656661">were suspended</a> <a href="https://www.americamagazine.org/news/2016/02/23/nicaragua-jesuit-fernando-cardenal-dies-82/">over their work</a> in Sandinista Nicaragua.</p>

<p>John Paul ordered that the Peruvian bishops begin an investigation of Gutiérrez – above all, over <a href="https://www.ncronline.org/news/theology/vatican-doctrinal-czar-liberation-theology-pioneer-reflects-troubles">Marxism’s influence on his work</a>. Gutiérrez was ultimately not punished. </p>

<p>One factor in his favor may have been his consistent opposition to armed revolution, even before violence raged in Peru from the 1980s into the ’90s. <a href="https://www.dukeupress.edu/Shining-and-Other-Paths">The Shining Path</a>, a Maoist guerrilla group, was waging a war of terrorism against the Peruvian government, setting off bombs across Peru. </p>

<p>Under President Alberto Fujimori, the government escalated existing counterinsurgency operations, often using indiscriminate violence against citizens in the region where the Shining Path emerged. In 2009, Fujimori was convicted of <a href="https://academic.oup.com/ijtj/article-abstract/3/3/384/2888395?redirectedFrom=fulltext">human rights violations</a>.</p>

<h2>Young priest</h2>

<p>Leo has never described himself as a liberationist Catholic. However, his experiences as a priest were <a href="https://www.nybooks.com/online/2026/05/24/the-education-of-pope-leo-xiv/">indelibly shaped by liberation theology</a>, the Peruvian armed conflict and the church debates that roiled much of Latin America during his years there.</p>

<p>Leo, born Robert Prevost, was raised in Chicago. After ordination, his journey as a priest began in Peru, where he landed for missionary work in 1985. The young friar followed in the footsteps of other <a href="https://undpress.nd.edu/9780268029050/maryknoll-catholic-mission-in-peru-1943-1989/">U.S. Catholic missionaries</a> who had been serving among Peru’s poor and Indigenous, urban and rural, since the 1940s.</p>

<p>Sent to Chulucanas, in Peru’s coastal northwest, Prevost found himself in a region of pastoral experimentation. Since the 1960s, Augustinian missionaries had been <a href="https://www.nybooks.com/online/2026/05/24/the-education-of-pope-leo-xiv/">working closely</a> with the community to provide literacy education, discussion groups about poverty and inequality, and workshops to train artisans. </p>

<p>These programs were a far cry from the more radical actions of some Catholics who supported liberation theology. Nevertheless, the programs in Chulucanas aimed to empower the Peruvian poor, chipping away at exploitation and low wages on the region’s sugarcane and cotton estates. Like Gutiérrez, many Peruvian Christians believed that the Shining Path <a href="https://doi.org/10.1179/1462317X13Z.0000000004">drew support because of pervasive poverty and inequality</a>, and that churches could help transform the nation. </p>

<p>But the Catholic Church in Latin America was in the midst of another transformation. John Paul gradually appointed <a href="https://www.routledge.com/The-Politics-of-Transnational-Actors-in-Latin-America-Power-from-Afar/Shepherd/p/book/9781138096332">conservative bishops</a> across the continent. Experimental pastoral programs lost support, and institutions that trained priests to put liberation theology into action, such as the <a href="https://doi.org/10.13016/4bla-77sh">Regional Seminary of the Southeast</a> in Mexico, were shuttered or “reoriented.” </p>

<p>Yet even as the hierarchy shifted conservative, work on the ground among Latin America’s poorest continued apace. From <a href="https://press.umich.edu/Books/D/Divined-Intervention2">coffee cooperatives in Mexico</a> to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1515/9783111726069">human rights activists</a> across the continent, many programs survived.</p>

<h2>‘Cease the repression’</h2>

<p>Leo’s 2026 itinerary includes multiple stops that speak to this history and on-the-ground pastoral work. The most symbolic, perhaps, is the Capilla San Óscar Romero, located in Chiclayo, the pope’s former diocese.</p>

<p>A neighborhood chapel <a href="https://www.latintimes.com/pope-leo-xiv-visit-chiclayo-chapel-600527">renovated with donations</a> from Leo’s connections in the United States, it is one of many sites throughout the Americas honoring Catholics who fell victim to right-wing, anti-communist violence. The day before Romero’s assassination, he used his weekly radio address to speak directly to El Salvador’s conscripted soldiers, telling them, “<a href="https://sojo.net/magazine/may-1980/pastors-last-homily">No soldier is obliged to obey an order counter to the law of God</a>.”</p>

<p>Leo XIV’s visit to the chapel is for private prayer, not a homily or a speech. Still, I would argue that the soft-spoken pope’s stop will evoke Romero’s message – especially at a time of <a href="https://apnews.com/article/rubio-peru-drug-trafficking-trump-b625fe79a901799707343ff5dd83b5f4">strikes against suspected drug traffickers</a>, which <a href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2025/09/18/us-maritime-strikes-amount-to-extrajudicial-killings">human rights groups</a> have <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/ck5ye7v88qy7o">criticized as extrajudicial killings</a>. <a href="https://sojo.net/magazine/may-1980/pastors-last-homily">During his final Mass</a>, Romero pleaded, “I beseech you, I beg you, I command you in the name of God: Cease the repression!”</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294299/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: A mototaxi drives past a banner of Pope Leo XIV in Chiclayo, Peru, on Nov. 5, 2026, ahead of his trip to Latin America
AP Photo/Martin Mejia Pope Leo XIV travels to Latin America on Nov. 6, 2026, with a packed itinerary that will bring him through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru
It is Leo’s first trip to the region since his elevation to the papacy – and a homecoming for a pope who spent two decades in Peru and holds Peruvian citizenship
As a historian of Catholicism in the late 20th century , I couldn’t help but notice that the pope’s plans walk a fine line during a fraught political moment in Latin America
Leo plans to meet with the right-wing presidents of Argentina and Peru
He will also visit sites often associated with the progressive wing of the Catholic Church, including Casavalle, one of the poorest neighborhoods in Uruguay’s capital
In Argentina, where President Javier Milei has drastically cut funding for disability services, the pope will go to a Catholic home for disabled people
And in Chiclayo, Peru, where Leo served as a bishop, he will pray at a chapel dedicated to St. Óscar Romero
A Salvadoran archbishop, Romero was assassinated in 1980 after years of speaking out against the human rights violations committed by the U.S.-supported Salvadoran military
His ministry was influenced by liberation theology , a controversial movement born in Peru that roiled church politics for decades – including during Leo’s years in Peru
Oscar Romero during a religious procession honoring him in San Salvador, El Salvador, on Aug. 1, 2024
AP Photo/Salvador Melendez What is liberation theology? The name itself was coined in a 1968 lecture by Gustavo Gutiérrez , a Peruvian theologian and priest
He expanded on his ideas in a 1971 book, “ A Theology of Liberation .” Gutiérrez and like-minded theologians argued that Christians have a moral duty to liberate the oppressed
They saw poverty, violence, racism and discrimination as not just problems but collective sins

While building on earlier Catholic social teachings, these “liberationists” envisioned profound change that went beyond the spiritual care and charitable work of traditional Latin American Catholicism

Catholics inspired by liberation theology created community organizations and work cooperatives, organized labor unions and fostered other initiatives that sought to measurably improve the lives of the poor
In my own research , I’ve documented how priests and nuns in rural Mexico helped organize transportation, corn milling and carpentry cooperatives
Gustavo Gutiérrez’s writings provided the foundation for liberation theology in the 1960s and ’70s
Bettmann/Getty Images Gutiérrez also argued that Christians should use Marxist ideas about analyzing society and the economy to better understand inequality

In nations like Peru, which possessed rich natural resources , liberationists tailored their economic justice projects to address how international and national companies profited off the low wages of miners and farmers
During the Cold War, however, these ideas led some politicians and church leaders to accuse liberationists of socialism and communism
A minority fringe of liberationists did embrace left-ring radicalism
Christians for Socialism , for example, argued that liberation meant rejecting capitalism
Some clergy, although only a handful, even picked up arms to fight alongside clandestine left-wing revolutionary groups
A wary pope This presented a dilemma to the Vatican
In 1891, Pope Leo XIII – the current pope’s namesake – published “Rerum Novarum ,” an encyclical focused on workers’ rights amid the Industrial Revolution
Since then, the Vatican had critiqued the worst excesses of capitalism while also rejecting socialism and communism, which it viewed as godless ideologies
During the 1960s and ’70s, Pope Paul VI generally supported local initiatives by liberationist Catholics , including some in Chulucanas, Peru , where Leo began his missionary work
Paul appointed and elevated bishops who shared a vision that the church could help empower the poor and alleviate oppression
But the Vatican shifted when the Polish cardinal Karol Józef Wojtyla became Pope John Paul II in 1978
For most of his adult life, Poland had been part of the Soviet bloc, which imposed restrictions on organized religion
A staunch opponent of communism , he worried about liberation theology’s use of Marxist analysis
So did one of his top Vatican officials, Joseph Ratzinger – the future Pope Benedict XVI
Pope John Paul II prays at the tomb of anti-communist dissident priest Jerzy Popieluszko, in front of the Church of St
Jean-Claude Delmas/AFP via Getty Images The Vatican began investigating some liberation theologians for violations of church teachings

In 1985, for example, Brazilian liberationist theologian Leonardo Boff was ordered to observe a year of silence – no publishing, no public speaking – to discipline him for his critique of the church’s hierarchy
Several priests were suspended over their work in Sandinista Nicaragua
John Paul ordered that the Peruvian bishops begin an investigation of Gutiérrez – above all, over Marxism’s influence on his work
One factor in his favor may have been his consistent opposition to armed revolution, even before violence raged in Peru from the 1980s into the ’90s
The Shining Path , a Maoist guerrilla group, was waging a war of terrorism against the Peruvian government, setting off bombs across Peru

title: Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms stands on the shoulders of Stacey Abrams, Charlotta Bass and countless other Black women who dreamed
